items.title: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report)
items.description: Renters comfortably affording a house would need a $14,408 raise to buy one (October Rent Report) Rental demand is up 22% as buying a single-family home stretches the budget far further than renting one. Written by Kara Ng on November 12, 2026 A household that can comfortably afford to rent a single-family home would need a $14,408 annual raise to afford the monthly costs of owning a home. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, as measured by the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index, with demand for single-family rentals up 24.3%. The typical U.S. single-family rent was $2,243 a month in October, up 3.2% from a year ago, while the typical multifamily rent was $1,744, up 2.5%, according to the Zillow Observed Rent Index. Wanting a more suburban lifestyle — the extra space, yard and private garage that often come with a single-family home — doesn’t always mean stretching the budget to buy. In fact, it’s a stretch most families aren’t prepared to make, especially when a household comfortably affording the rent for a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. To comfortably afford those costs — the rule of thumb being to spend no more than 30% of its income on housing — a household needs an income of $89,724 to rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a choice and not a fallback. It takes less income than owning, and it leaves more room in the monthly budget. The size of the raise depends on the market The pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline — the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead — at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). items.title: Existing-Home Sales Decreased 5.5% in October, According to NAR Report
items.description: Existing-Home Sales Decreased 5.5% in October, According to NAR Report Section Menu NAR Media Contacts Statistical Release Schedule Op-Eds & Letters to the Editor NAR Fact Sheet NAR in the News More November 12, 2026 Media Contact: Media Relations Mortgages & Home Financing , Financing & Credit , Residential Real Estate Share View and share infographic Month-Over-Month Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October. Unsold inventory increased 1.3% to 1.59 million units, equal to a 5.1-month supply. Year-Over-Year Existing-home sales decreased 8.8%. The median existing-home sales price increased 0.4% to $416,700. WASHINGTON (November 12, 2026) – Existing-home sales decreased by 5.5% month-over-month and decreased by 8.8% year-over-year, according to the National Association of REALTORS® Existing-Home Sales report. The report provides the real estate ecosystem, including agents, homebuyers and sellers, with data on the level of home sales, price and inventory. Month-over-month sales declined in the Midwest, South and West and held steady in the Northeast. Year-over-year sales declined in all four regions. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation. The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2% of all transactions,” Yun said. “Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.” National Snapshot Total Existing-Home Sales for October Existing-home sales decreased 5.5% month-over-month. 1 Existing-home sales decreased 8.8% year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million. Inventory in October Total housing inventory was 1.59 million units, up 1.3% from September and 4.6% from October 2025. 2 Unsold inventory represented a 5.1-month supply, up from 4.7 months in September and 4.4 months in October 2025. Median Sales Price in October The median existing-home price for all housing types was $416,700. 3 The median price increased 0.4% from $414,900 one year ago, marking the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases. Housing Affordability in October The Housing Affordability Index registered at 100.7, down from 107.3 one year ago. Year-over-year, affordability declined in all four regions. The median home price was $421,900, up 0.4% from one year ago. Condominiums and Co-ops in October Sales decreased 2.9% month-over-month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 340,000. Sales were down 10.5% from one year ago. The median price was $365,100, up 0.3% from October 2025. The median price was $360,900, down 0.4% from October 2025. West Sales decreased 9.7% month-over-month to an annual rate of 650,000. Sales were down 14.5% year-over-year. The median price was $624,300, unchanged from October 2025. REALTORS® Confidence Index for October The median time on market was 35 days, up from 33 days in September and 34 days in October 2025. First-time homebuyers accounted for 29% of sales, down from 31% in September and 32% in October 2025. Cash sales accounted for 29% of transactions, up from 27% in September and unchanged from October 2025. Individual investors and second-home buyers accounted for 20% of transactions, unchanged from September and up from 16% in October 2025. Distressed sales accounted for 2% of sales, unchanged from September and October 2025. 4 Mortgage Rates The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.33% in October, according to Freddie Mac, up from 6.86% in September and 6.25% one year ago. items.title: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS
items.description: OCTOBER CHILL BRINGS COOLER SALES, MORE CHOICES FOR HOUSTON BUYERS Home prices hold steady as supply reaches a 14-year high HOUSTON -- (November 11, 2026) -- The Greater Houston housing market saw a change in pace in October, offering buyers more choices while sellers adjusted to a shift in activity. According to the Houston Association of Realtors' October 2026 Housing Market Update, single-family home sales were 14.9% below last year's level, with 6,348 homes sold. The average home price held steady in October at $421,100, while the median price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. The number of homes on the market remained near record levels, with 40,253 single-family homes for sale, up 6.8% from last October. "Consumers are paying close attention to the economy and their household budgets, so it is understandable that some buyers are taking more time before purchasing a home," said HAR Chair Theresa Hill with Compass RE Texas, LLC - Houston. "We typically see activity ease as the year winds down, but buyers who are still looking may have more time to find a home that fits their needs and budget." Housing Market Overview Across all property types, 7,485 properties were sold in October, down 15.1% compared with a year earlier. Total dollar volume dipped 14.6% to $3.06 billion. The number of active listings across all property types increased 4.8% to 61,965 Despite October's decline, single-family home sales through the first 10 months of 2026 remained within 2% of last year's pace. Stronger sales during the spring and early summer helped offset the declines recorded in recent months. Single-Family Homes Update In October, 6,348 single-family homes sold across the Houston area, compared with 7,458 during the same time last year. That represents a decline of 14.9%. October's single-family home sales were the fewest for any October in the past 10 years. However, total sales over the prior 12 months reached 87,433, remaining above the 2019 level of 85,685, the last normal year before the pandemic. The average price was virtually unchanged at $421,100. The median price was $320,000, which is 3.0% below last year's level. It is the lowest median price for any October since 2021, with an October peak of $335,000 in 2024. The average mortgage rate in October was 7.33%, up 108 basis points from a year ago, but still below the 7.62% recorded in October 2023. Buyers of a median-priced home paid an estimated monthly mortgage payment (including principal and interest) of $1,760.28. That is $134.79 more than a year ago but less than the $1,845.03 paid in October 2023, when both rates and median home prices were higher. "Affordability remains a challenge for homebuyers, and the possibility of a quarter-point interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve before the end of the year could add further pressure to the housing market," said HAR Chief Economist Ted C. Jones. Homes spent an average of 59 days on the market, unchanged from last October. Pending sales, which represent homes under contract but not yet sold, declined 17.6% to 6,445. The market had a 5.5-month supply of single-family homes, unchanged from September and its highest level since 2012. Nationwide, there was a 4.8 months' supply, according to the National Association of Realtors. Broken out by housing segments, single-family home sales performed as follows: $1 - $99,999: increased 2.1% (97 transactions) $100,000 - $149,999: decreased 1.0% (191 transactions) $150,000 - $249,999: decreased 9.4% (1,339 transactions) $250,000 - $499,999: decreased 16.8% (3,368 transactions) $500,000 - $999,999: decreased 16.9% (1,061 transactions) $1M and above: decreased 11.6% (291 transactions) HAR also reports on existing single-family home sales, which fell 10.2% in October. The average price declined slightly to $428,790, while the median price was down 4.5% to $315,000. HAR will publish its October 2026 Rental Market Update on Wednesday, November 18. For HAR's Monthly Activity Snapshot of the October 2026 trends, please CLICK HERE to access a downloadable PDF file. Townhome/Condominium Update The townhome and condominium market also recorded fewer sales in October. Sales declined 23.5% year over year, with 336 properties sold compared with 439 last October. The average sales price increased 5.8% to $263,413, while the median price declined 3.7% to $197,500. Active listings climbed 5.6% to 3,586 properties. The supply of townhomes and condominiums expanded from 8.2 months to 9.4 months, while days on market edged up to 65 days. Houston Real Estate Highlights in October Single-family home sales declined 14.9% year over year. Pending single-family sales declined 17.6% to 6,445. Active single-family listings increased 6.8% to 40,253. The average single-family home price was flat at $421,100. The median single-family home price declined 3.0% to $320,000, its lowest level since January 2024. Single-family homes took an average of 59 days to sell, unchanged from last year. The supply of single-family homes increased from 5.1 months to 5.5 months. Total property sales declined 15.1%, with 7,485 transactions. Total dollar volume declined 14.6% to $3.06 billion. items.title: October 2026 Hottest Housing Markets
items.description: October 2026 Hottest Housing Markets By Hannah Jones Nov 13, 2026 Highlights Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Conn. claimed the top spot in October for the first time since a summer run on top from May – July 2026. Buyer demand remains highly concentrated in the hottest markets, where listings attracted 2.6 times the national average number of views per property. The Midwest and Northeast were the only regions represented in the Top 20 for the 37th consecutive month. The list was evenly split this month, with 10 markets in the Midwest and 10 in the Northeast. Homes in the hottest markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on market of 37 days, more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm. Among large U.S. metros, Jacksonville, FL posted the biggest year-over-year improvement, jumping 70 spots to rank 189th nationally. The Hartford, CT metro moved up one spot from last month to claim the top spot on the hottest housing markets list for the first time since the summer. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, but has claimed the top spot only eight times. Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country. In October, Hartford attracted 4.1 times the national average number of viewers per property. Homes sold in just 37 days, one day slower than a year ago but almost a month faster than the national norm. At a median listing price of $440,000, Hartford is priced just above the national norm, in a region generally priced well-above. Realtor.com’s Market Hotness rankings take into account two aspects of the housing market: 1) market demand, as measured by unique views per property on Realtor.com, and 2) the pace of the market as measured by the number of days a listing remains active on Realtor.com. ($549,000) is also priced below the regional norm. Connecticut accounts for four of the Top 20 markets, with Waterbury-Shelton, New Haven and Norwich joining Hartford at median list prices between $400,000 and $460,000. Springfield, Mass. and Rochester, N.Y. are priced below the national norm and well below the Northeast’s. New England’s compact geography is part of the draw. Hartford, New Haven, Waterbury and Springfield sit within roughly an hour’s drive of one another, so buyers can compare neighborhoods and price points across several metros without leaving the region. That flexibility concentrates demand, and inventory in these markets remains well below pre-pandemic norms. The pull shows up in buyer traffic, with all six New England markets on the list drawing at least 2.6 times the national average views per property, at or above the Top 20 average. For shoppers, widening the search within the region means more options but not much relief from competition, since the affordability that draws buyers to one market is drawing them to its neighbors as well. Most Improved Large Markets Large markets showed renewed momentum in October, moving up the list by 6 spots on average compared to last year. This suggests that big-city markets, while still trailing smaller and more affordable alternatives, are capturing renewed attention as buyers weigh the tradeoffs between affordability and access to larger job centers, especially as home prices soften across much of the country. Jacksonville, Fla. led all large markets with the biggest ranking improvement, climbing 70 spots year over year, while San Francisco and Denver posted notable gains of 38 and 33 spots respectively. Riverside jumped 32 spots, and Sacramento rounded out the top five most improved, advancing 31 spots. The biggest movers were still fairly low on the overall list, ranging from 73rd for San Francisco to 216th for Denver. Four of the five biggest movers were located in the West, with three in California and one in the South. Though the South and West remain outside the nation's hottest markets, some areas are beginning to show growing demand and faster time-on-market. San Francisco stands out, with homes selling more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm, an acceleration likely boosted by the area’s ongoing AI boom . items.title: Freddie Mac rates dip again this week, but sticky inflation could erase the relief
items.description: Freddie Mac rates dip again this week, but sticky inflation could erase the relief By Jiayi Xu Nov 12, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate declined 7 basis points to 7.11% this week, its fourth straight weekly decline. Even so, it remains 87 basis points above a year ago, and the downtrend trend could potentially reverse next week as the 10-year yield returns to 5%. The strong October jobs report showed the labor market holding up well, clearing the way for the Fed’s next rate hike. On Tuesday morning, before the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a larger 50-basis-point move should be considered in December’s meeting if inflation came in hot. Shortly afterward, the October CPI report came in hotter than forecast, pushing the 10-year Treasury yield toward 5%. A December hike is now essentially priced in. The debate is no longer if the Fed hikes, but how far and how fast. What does this mean for the housing market? Today’s homebuyers are squeezed by both high mortgage rates and high inflation, and inflation is the bigger long-term problem. High rates raise monthly payments and shrink the loan a buyer can qualify for, and the recent pullback in pending sales shows how sensitive buyers are . But persistent high inflation is what keeps the Fed hiking and rates elevated. Inflation also leaves households with less to put toward a home, especially when wages lag prices. First-time buyers feel it most. With no equity to lean on, they must save a down payment from budgets already stretched thin. Even if rates ease, living costs rising faster than pay will keep weighing on demand for years.

items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 7, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Nov. 7, 2026) By Hannah Jones Nov 12, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows Though mortgage rates have fallen for the last three consecutive weeks, they remain in 7%+ territory, impacting both buyer and seller willingness to participate in the market. With rates roughly 1 percentage point above year-ago levels, buyers have seen their buying power diminish, even as easing listing prices have worked in favor of affordability. Sellers have responded to cooling buyer demand by pulling back on listing activity. New listing activity has fallen for the last six weeks, and dipped by double digits this week. Time on market has remained relatively stable as easing activity from both the buyer and seller sides of the market have dropped the baseline of activity, but left the market pace largely steady. The typical mortgage holder in the U.S. would face a more than $1,000 increase in their monthly mortgage payment if they were to buy a median-priced home at today’s prevailing mortgage rate. This jump discourages seller activity, especially as lackluster buyer demand may mean dropping their asking price well below their ideal level to drum up buyer attention. With both buyers and sellers showing signs of retreat, the housing market could enter its annual winter freeze early this year. Active inventory climbed 8.3% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.3% compared to a year ago, continuing a string of strong inventory growth since the summer. Inventory has been building momentum since July, rising from roughly 2% year-over-year growth in mid-July to more than 8% now. However, this pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers, but by a pullback in buyer activity. Year-to-date, active inventory i s up 5.0%. Homes spent 1 day longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 65 days, with homes selling one day slower than the same time last year. This marks the third week in a row that time on market has slowed after a long stretch reaching back to May of homes selling at the same pace or faster than last year. As mortgage rates top 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 10.3% year-over-year New listing activity took another sharp turn downward this week, dropping 10.3% year over year. Sellers are discouraged because of how disengaged buyers are. The prices buyers are open to are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower. The gap between the typical outstanding mortgage rate and the prevailing rate has grown, making relocating a less attractive proposition. The stronger new listing activity earlier in the year has the year-to-date change at -0.6%. The median listing price fell 1.2% year-over-year The median listing price dropped just below $410,000, down 1.2% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 43 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.1% year over year. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch that has lowered the price they are willing to pay. Sellers have responded to this shift, but not enough to get the market moving. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: Rapid absorption continues even as deliveries slow for the Phoenix multifamily market
items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Phoenix multifamily market report here.Highlights:Operating conditions in the Phoenix multifamily market improved during the third quarter, continuing patterns from the first half of this year. While property fundamentals have improved, investment activity has slowed in recent months.Vacancy dipped by 10 basis points in the third quarter, following steeper declines in the first half of the year. The current vacancy rate for stabilized properties is 6.5%, 70 basis points lower than levels from one year earlier.Area rents have gained ground in each of the first three quarters of 2026, although gains have been modest and current rents are still down slightly compared to one year ago. Rents ended the third quarter at $1,524 per month.Sales activity slowed in the third quarter, particularly among properties that have been delivered in recent years. items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. items.title: Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges – RISmedia
items.description: Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals Single-family rental demand is rising nationwide, with demand up 24.3% year over year as the cost of homeownership continues to outpace renting. Home Agents November 12, 2026, 3 pm Reading Time: 3 mins read Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.” The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). For more information, visit www.zillow.com . The median home sales price declined 6.9% to $404,802 following months of relatively stable pricing, which can be attributed to lower-priced homes accounting for a greater share of sales. Demand remained strongest among homes priced between $200,000 and $299,000, underscoring how affordability continues to shape buyer activity. Vaike O'Grady, market research advisor at Unlock MLS, said affordability challenges continue to weigh on the Central Texas housing market, even as resale homes become more competitive with new construction. “Despite another softer month, year-to-date home sales are up 2.5% compared with the same period last year, and while overall pending sales declined 4.0% year over year, pending resale contracts increased 6%. Builders have relied on incentives such as price reductions and mortgage rate buydowns to attract buyers, but that competitive advantage may be narrowing. This shift suggests resale activity is gaining traction as buyers continue to weigh affordability and value in their homebuying decisions.” John Crowe , 2026 Unlock MLS and ABoR president, emphasized that softer home prices and slower sales may give buyers greater negotiating flexibility, while sellers must remain competitive with their pricing and expectations. “The data is an important starting point, but understanding the factors behind the numbers is what helps buyers and sellers determine when the time is right for them. A professional agent can help buyers and sellers understand what's driving market trends, how conditions differ by county and what this all means for making their next move. items.title: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October
items.description: Annual rent growth sees a milestone, even as prices ease in October by Kim O'Brien Posted November 6, 2026 in Market Research October marked the first month of rent cuts in the U.S. apartment market in 2026, but annual gains continue at a robust pace. Same-store effective asking rents increased 1.7% year-over-year, according to October data from RealPage Market Analytics . That was the market’s biggest annual price increase since May 2023. While the annual reading has improved, the gain stemmed less from robust monthly pricing and more from weak rent performance falling out of the annual calculation. In fact, rents came down a mild 0.7% during October, marking the first monthly rent cut in the U.S. in calendar 2026. U.S. apartment occupancy faded to 95% in October, easing 20 basis points (bps) from the September showing. Still, October occupancy is up 40 bps in the calendar year and remains 10 bps ahead of the October 2025 showing. Helping support occupancy and rent performance, the U.S. apartment market has seen supply and demand edge closer to balance recently. Renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, gaining ground on a cooling supply wave. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units in the past year, nearly half the recent peak from late 2024. Bay Area and Midwest markets still lead for rent growth Rent performance remained sharply split by market. Coastal tech hubs and Midwest metros delivered the strongest annual gains, while most Sun Belt markets kept logging rent declines. Northern California's tech-driven markets posted the three strongest gains among the 50 largest apartment markets in the year-ending October. San Francisco saw rents hike 14.7% over the past year, San Jose followed at 9.5%, and Oakland reached 8.5%. All three markets are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest markets make up much of the rest of the top 10 list. Milwaukee led the major Midwest markets with annual rent growth of 4.2%, followed by Chicago (3.3%), Kansas City (3.1%) and Cleveland (3.1%). Detroit and St. Louis both fell just shy of making the cut, with annual rent growth of 2.7% in each market. Sun Belt rents still trail, but the gap is narrowing The South region overall has returned to annual rent growth, though barely, at 0.5% in October. Sun Belt and Florida markets continue to see the nation’s steepest declines. San Antonio had the deepest cut among big markets at 2.6%, stemming from occupancy at 92.5%, also dead last among the largest 50 markets. Also posting rent declines in the year-ending October were Houston (-1.8%), Tampa (-1%), Charlotte (-0.9%) and Denver (-0.8%). The bigger story, however, is how many Sun Belt markets have stopped seeing rent positioning hemorrhage. Annual increases have returned to Phoenix (0.4%) and Austin (0.6%), as well as Atlanta (0.8%), Raleigh (1.0%), Miami (0.6%) and Jacksonville (2.6%). Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: The cost of 30 years of certainty
items.description: As mortgage rates top 7%, buyers increasingly turn to adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for monthly savings despite future reset risks. Upfront savings: A 5/1 ARM lowers initial rates by ~1%, saving ~$3,900 annually on a $500,000 loan. Volume surge: ARMs now account for 20% of mortgage dollar volume, led by high-cost states. Strong credit profile: Serious delinquency on post-2010 ARMs sits below 0.5%, proving more resilient than fixed-rate loans There is now a nearly $4,000 annual difference between paying for a $500,000 home with a fixed-rate mortgage and an adjustable-rate mortgage. That figure only grows alongside price. As affordability pushes buyers to make sacrifices, Cotality data shows that there’s been an increase in the number of buyers taking advantage of those extra funds afforded by adjustable-rate mortgages. The savings secured with these flexible mortgages is meaningful, but it’s not stable. “Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down,” said Cotality Principal Economist Archana Pradhan, “They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results.” An ARM to lean on Conventional wisdom has historically pushed buyers toward adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) when rates are rising. The thinking goes: lock in a rate for 5, 7, or 10 years and then refinance before the mortgage’s fixed period ends. That logic still holds appeal. With current mortgage rates above 7%, people taking out a conventional mortgage today will have a higher rate than most current homeowners; Cotality data shows only 28% of mortgages have interest rates above 5%. Taking out a 5-year ARM at current rates would drop a borrower’s interest rate down around a full point. Accordingly, a full 20% of mortgage dollar volumes are allocated to ARMs, according to Cotality data. However, if the rate adjusts upward following a fixed period, it can quickly eat away at earlier savings. And that reality is a distinct possibility. Cotality economists anticipate that current rates reflect a new normal rather than an anomaly. “Since the 2010s, rates have hovered around 2 to 5 basis points below where they are today. And then pandemic-era rates reset expectations to unrealistic levels,” said Pradhan. “People taking out ARMs today shouldn’t expect the rock-bottom-rates of 2020-2022 when they refinance down the road.” A refinance at the wrong time risks leaving someone exposed to larger monthly payments — and possible default. Buyers are taking a bet as affordability wears them down. They’re choosing available cash in the short term over a guarantee of consistent payments down the road. That solution has very market-dependent results. Archana Pradhan Cotality Principal Economist The price of popularity Affordability is pushing many buyers to the edge. Cotality tracks how homebuyers feel about price pressures , and in a recent survey , 69% of buyers said they were willing to cut lifestyle spending to afford a home. Sixty-five percent seek smaller mortgages for lower monthly payments. Buyers’ eagerness to take on ARMs underscores how strained they are; a few hundred dollars can make the difference between ending the month in the black or the red. Should an adjustable rate mortgage term come up for renewal, current rates could tip monthly payments past the point where homeowners’ finances can absorb the increase. However, Cotality data shows that ARMs are not any more prone to mortgage delinquencies than conventional mortgages. Adjustable-rate mortgages originated after 2010 have a strong track record. Only 0.5% of ARMs from this category are seriously delinquent (90 days or more late), which is slightly lower than fixed rate loans. Even during the economic disruption of early 2020, adjustable mortgages saw serious delinquencies top out at 3.0% as compared to around 3.5% for fixed-rate loans. That’s because households rarely let the mortgage go at the first sign of trouble. Instead, they find room elsewhere in the budget, a trend recorded in Cotality survey data. Sixty-five percent of homebuyers will take out a smaller mortgage to lower monthly payments. For the Gen Z buyers, that figure is 82%. But a smaller mortgage isn’t always possible. In high-cost areas like Washington State, California, and New York, average home prices are $255,000, $324,000, $269,000 above the national average, according to Cotality data. Transactions haven’t slowed, buyers have just become increasingly dependent on ARM loans. More homeowners are looking to make that room by reducing monthly payments, and adjustable-rate mortgages provide a way to do so without tightening the belt elsewhere. As margins become thinner, and as people look for ways to enter the market even at higher rates, alternative mortgage types provide a pathway forward. items.title: Monthly Mortgage Payments Fall to Lowest Level in 6 Weeks as Home Prices Keep Dipping
items.description: Monthly Mortgage Payments Fall to Lowest Level in 6 Weeks as Home Prices Keep Dipping Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson Pending home sales held steady from a week earlier as prices and mortgage rates fell–but rates have since ticked back up. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending November 8: Home-sale prices fell for the fourth week in a row. The median home-sale price was $388,613, down 0.9% year over year. That’s four straight weeks of declines after three years of increases, handing homebuyers a bit of relief on top of what they’re getting from dipping rates. Monthly housing payments dropped to a 6-week low. The median monthly mortgage payment was $2,755 at a 7.18% mortgage rate, the weekly average. This data is seasonally adjusted. Payments are down from $2,820 a month earlier. Homebuying activity held steady. Pending home sales were essentially flat (-0.1%) from a week earlier, though they remain at the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. Dipping mortgage rates likely held off a bigger decline in pending sales. Daily average rates declined to a 6-week low of 7.17% last week, but have since ticked back up after a hot inflation report . Overall supply held steady, too. Active listings were flat from a week earlier, while new listings slipped 1.3%. Buyers still have plenty of options; there are half a million more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. Condo buyers have especially strong negotiating power; condo sellers outnumber buyers more than 2 to 1. items.title: Inflation Persists in October
items.description: Inflation Persists in October November 10, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments Inflation remained elevated in October even as energy prices eased, raising expectations of another Fed rate hike. Shelter returned as the largest driver of headline inflation, accounting for over 30% of the monthly increase. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, rose by 0.3% for the third consecutive month, suggesting broad-based price pressures across the economy. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not release the annual inflation figure this month as October 2025 data is unavailable for comparison due to last year’s government shutdown. On a monthly basis, the CPI rose by 0.4% in October (seasonally adjusted), while the “core” CPI increased by 0.3%. The monthly increase in core CPI has remained at 0.3% since August. The price index for a broad set of energy sources increased by 0.7% in October, as decline in natural gas (-0.8%) was offset by increases in fuel oil (+2.0%), gasoline (+1.0%) and electricity (+0.9%). Meanwhile, the food at home and food away from home indexes rose by 0.4% and 0.5% respectively. Outside of energy, other top contributors that rose in October included indexes for recreation (+%), medical care (+0.3%), motor vehicle insurance (+0.7%), household furnishings and operations (+0.2%) and education (+0.3%). Meanwhile, the indexes for used cars and trucks (-1.2%) and communication (-0.1%) were among the major indexes that decreased over the month. The index for shelter, which makes up more than 40% of the “core” CPI, rose by 0.3% in October, following the same increase last month. The index for owners’ equivalent rent (OER) and rent of primary residence (RPR) increased by 0.3% and 0.2% over the month. NAHB constructs a “real” rent index to indicate whether inflation in rents is faster or slower than core inflation. It provides insight into the supply and demand conditions for rental housing. When inflation in rents is rising faster than core inflation, the real rent index rises and vice versa. The real rent index is calculated by dividing the price index for rent by the core CPI (to exclude the volatile food and energy components). In October, the Real Rent Index fell by 0.1%. items.description: Hot inflation report puts Fed on track for December rate hike By Kyle Campbell CloseText About Kyle twitter ByKyleCampbell Published November 10, 2026, 8:53 a.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 9:38 a.m. EST 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. Bloomberg News Key insight: The latest CPI inflation report, which showed inflation rising 0.4% in October, puts more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates. Recent comments suggest policymakers will be ready to hike. Expert quote: " I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." — Fed Gov. Christopher Waller Inflation rose faster than expected last month as lower energy costs could not offset broader price increases, according to Tuesday's consumer price index report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, rising 0.4% on the month. Processing Content The October CPI reading exceeded the consensus market forecast which expected a monthly increase of 0.24%. The Bureau of Labor Statistics did not issue an October CPI report last year, so the agency did not publish an annualized rate of inflation for last month. The print is better than September, when prices rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year, but hints at a troubling trend of accelerating inflation. Ahead of the report, Federal Open Market Committee members were already expressing increased concern about prices. Hours before the report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said his baseline expectation was that inflation would improve from September but the committee will still raise its benchmark interest rate a quarter percentage point next month. Even if inflation had come in below 0.3%, Waller said in a pre-written speech delivered in London, he would have backed a 25 basis point hike. With the October reading coming in above that level, he could support a bigger increase. "I am leaning toward supporting an increase in our policy rate of 25 basis points at the FOMC's December meeting," Waller said. "That's my plan if things proceed as I expect. But if the October CPI inflation data out later today are similar to the past two monthly readings … then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take." Waller joined the majority of FOMC voters in supporting their move to keep interest rates unchanged during the committee's meeting last month. In his speech he said this was appropriate because the group had already clearly signaled its intent to raise rates repeatedly, enabling market participants to price such a change into their valuation models. Yet, while the committee bought itself some flexibility in September, Waller said it must follow through on this "sooner rather than later" or else risk losing the trust of financial markets. Meanwhile, the Fed's other top priority, maintaining maximum employment, has been firmly in hand. The U.S. economy added 165,000 last month and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Waller is not the only Fed official who has called for tighter monetary policy. Two FOMC participants voted against last month's policy hold, Fed Gov. Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack, both of whom preferred a hike. Cook has yet to explain her rationale. Hammack, in a speech delivered in Zurich, Switzerland last week, noted that inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for nearly six years and has recently shown signs of broadening out beyond volatile food and energy prices. Because of this, she, too, anticipates monetary policy being tightened. "I expect that monetary policy will need to move to a restrictive stance to bring inflation back to 2% in a timely manner," Hammack said. "I prefer getting to that stance through more frequent smaller adjustments when possible, something which would be less disruptive to households, businesses, and financial markets." The two governors will not cast a vote next month, but they will be voting members of the committee next year, beginning in January. Three actions to drive ROI: 1) Refocus AI strategy around ROI that lasts against competition, 2) develop the ability to build agentic workflows and 3) double down on your own advantages. AI has spread through the commercial real estate industry at remarkable speed. Most investors now have access to it, and many can already see clear benefits: faster document processing, quicker analysis, easier report drafting. Far fewer can point to exactly how AI helps them achieve competitive advantage over their rivals. In a fast-moving market, improving from yesterday is not the same as pulling ahead. JLL’s 2026 Global Real Estate Investor AI Survey covers 800+ investors across 12 countries, spanning institutional, private and listed investors and investment management firms. In JLL’s 2025 Global Real Estate Technology Survey , 88% of respondents had started piloting AI or planned to start that year. By the end of 2026, 83% of investors have at least one activity area past the pilot stage, and 40% have every activity either scaling or fully embedded. This progress cuts across all seven activity areas. However, successful AI rollout is no longer a reliable signal for true maturity because Enterprise LLM licenses, such as Claude and ChatGPT, provide a “shortcut”. Unlike earlier enterprise software, they don’t require as much integration, configuration or process change before going live. A company can roll out AI access widely without changing how the work is done, and the survey suggests this is exactly what’s happening. items.title: Members Of Congress Have Questions For Brookfield After Its Mass Mobile Home Purchase
items.description: Brookfield quietly closed on the acquisition of the largest privately held manufactured housing portfolio in the United States this year, prompting some members of Congress to inquire about the investment giant’s plans for the properties it now owns. Bisnow/Ethan Rothstein Brookfield purchased Yes Communities from GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, in the second quarter, public filings and statements from Brookfield management indicate. Brookfield hasn’t publicized its acquisition of the Denver-based operator of nearly 300 manufactured home developments, but three Democrats from the House of Representatives nonetheless sent a letter to the firm last month voicing concern about the purchase and seeking pledges for tenant protections. Reps. Maxwell Alejandro Frost, Gabe Vasquez and Rashida Tlaib asked management at New York-based Brookfield Asset Management, the publicly traded arm of Toronto-based Brookfield, and Brookfield Real Estate Group to provide assurances that residents’ quality of life wouldn’t be impacted by the deal. The representatives gave BAM until Nov. 20 to respond. The asset management giant hadn’t yet replied as of mid-November, Frost’s office confirmed to Bisnow on Nov. 9. Brookfield didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment. It hasn’t formally announced the acquisition, which was first rumored to be in the works in September 2025, but BAM said in second-quarter filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it acquired “the largest privately held U.S. manufactured home portfolio.” Yes Communities operates more than 55,000 housing sites across the U.S., with a focus on the Southwest, Midwest and Southeast. A purchase price for the portfolio is unknown, but BAM said it spent $5.2B in the second quarter on its real estate business, including the manufactured home portfolio and the take-private of an industrial outdoor storage portfolio. Brookfield announced a $1.2B all-cash deal in February to buy Peakstone Realty Trust, a REIT with 60 IOS properties and 16 traditional industrial assets. In its second-quarter filings, Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust disclosed a new investment in a 2% ownership interest in 294 manufactured housing properties at a book value of $86.6M, which aligns with the number of properties under the Yes Communities banner. BAM Chief Financial Officer Hadley Peer Marshall also disclosed on the second-quarter earnings call that a Brookfield fund had made its first investment by deploying capital to Yes Communities. Other affiliates of Brookfield may have also contributed capital for the Yes Communities acquisition. Brookfield REIT said in an investor presentation on its website that as of Sept. 30, it owned a 294-community manufactured housing portfolio across 23 states, the same number of states Yes Communities is active in. Wikimedia Commons; Office of Maxwell Frost Democratic Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Gabriel Vasquez and Maxwell Frost have asked Brookfield about its acquisition of Yes Communities. Executives from Brookfield held one virtual meeting with residents and their advocates following the acquisition that was facilitated by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project and MHAction, two nonprofit advocacy groups, PESP confirmed to Bisnow . GIC and another unnamed institutional investor acquired a 71% equity interest in Yes Communities in 2016, with Stockbridge Capital Group holding on to the remaining stake. Brookfield was reportedly in talks with GIC about acquiring its stake for more than $10B, and it is unclear exactly the size of Brookfield's interest in Yes Communities or how much it paid. In their letter from Oct. 13, the three members of Congress sought details about the acquisition. The letter outlines previous tenants' complaints with Yes Communities for high rent increases, excessive fees and neglect of routine maintenance and says that Brookfield “has the opportunity to change this scenario” and “support meaningful protections for its residents.” “Given the challenges our constituents have experienced at Yes! properties, as well as broader concerns about the private equity business model, we seek assurances that Brookfield will prioritize improving residents’ quality of life and protecting their economic and housing stability, rather than exacerbating the economic challenges they already face,” the representatives wrote. The letter specifically asks Brookfield to disclose whether it plans to increase rents by more than 3% annually, to outline its policy regarding new and existing fees, and to confirm whether it will refrain from serial eviction filings for routine rent collection. The letter asks BAM to commit to meet regularly with tenants and to cooperate with tenant groups that are seeking to collectively purchase their communities. The housing legislation that made it to the president’s desk includes new restrictions on existing home purchases from institutional investors but carves out broad exemptions for new development of single-family communities built as rentals. items.title: Rising rents draw Wall Street money to industrial outdoor storage lot investments across the U.S.
items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Petrillo said that there is still plenty of room left for values to increase, so an investor jumping in now hasn't missed the game. "We are still in the very early innings," Petrillo said. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said. CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future. Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added. Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS. Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants. And institutional money is making IOS more competitive. "Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said. He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said. Published Nov. 9, 2026 Julie Strupp Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners broke ground Nov. 5 on ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, Calif. Courtesy of Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners Several multifamily projects broke ground around the country in the first week of November. Lincoln Property Co. and McCourt Partners started a development called ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, California, one of the strongest rental markets in Southern California, according to Stephen Lindgren, senior vice president and Los Angeles market leader at Lincoln. Like much of the SoCal region, Culver City needs more housing, but “as with any new housing development of this scale, the entitlement process and rising construction costs can present challenges,” Lindgren said in emailed comments. However, “Culver City leaders have recognized the need to create a supportive environment for new residential development,” Lindgren said. “That partnership has been instrumental in advancing ElevenOneEleven.” Here is more detail about the ElevenOneEleven project and two other newly launched developments in Texas and Pennsylvania. ElevenOneEleven in Culver City, California On Thursday, Lincoln and McCourt Partners started construction on a six-story, mixed-use development in the Los Angeles area close to major employers and “convenient access to the best West LA lifestyle amenities,” according to a press release shared with Multifamily Dive. The project price tag is $200 million , the Los Angeles Times reported. The development will bring 344 apartments, including 52 affordable units. items.title: Home trends you’ll see in 2027, according to Zillow
items.description: Home trends you’ll see in 2027, according to Zillow by Emily Marek November 10, 2026 Color drenching is likely to be one of the top home trends of 2027, with the keyword increasing 84% in listing descriptions on Zillow. (Image via Zillow) Quiet tech, elevated luxuries and color-drenched rooms will be among the most popular home trends in 2027, according to a new report from Zillow . The listing giant analyzed keywords in listing descriptions across its site to determine features that are increasingly desirable — and increasingly undesirable — to home shoppers. Since listing descriptions are a real-time indicator of how homes are being marketed, Zillow said, they offer a sneak peek of characteristics, designs and upgrades that are likely to take over home trends in the near future. With that in mind, here are the top home trends Zillow predicts for the upcoming year. Tech … and space to unplug from it While mentions of AI-powered appliances are up 119% year over year on Zillow, “spaces to unplug” have also jumped 34% as “digital detox” becomes an increasingly luxurious concept, said Zillow’s home trends expert, Amanda Pendleton. “Homes are getting smarter, but buyers also want tech-free zones where nothing needs charging. Sellers and their real estate agents are now highlighting spaces to unplug,” Pendleton said in a press release. “Taken together, this data suggests buyers value homes that are functional and efficient but still feel polished and personal.” ‘Elevated’ styling While listing descriptions show that buyers and homeowners still want their spaces to feel “cozy,” the up-and-coming trend is a more luxurious, polished feel. “Cozy” is still one of the most popular Zillow keywords, although mentions decreased 22% year over year, alongside words like “eclectic” (down 19%) and boho (down 13%). Instead, listings that mention “elevated” spaces and features increased 71%. Bold accents Specific trends within the elevated styling craze include color-drenched walls, which increased 84%; painted brick exteriors, which increased 27%; and board-and-batten walls and siding, which increased 24%. Efficiency Listings are now far less likely to mention sustainability features than they were over the past few years: Buzzwords like “sustainable” and “green” both fell 26% year over year. Instead, buyers now want to know that their home is efficient. Increasingly popular are behind-the-scenes features like fresh-air ventilation systems (up 52%), recirculating hot-water systems (up 52%), whole home batteries (up 43%), backup batteries (up 25%), air filtration (up 25%), water filtration (up 22%) and radon mitigation (up 18%). Multigenerational living spaces “ Multigenerational living ” is ever on the rise among today’s prospective homeowners, with the keyword jumping in popularity by 58%. Further indicators of the rise of multigenerational living — and the increasing age of today’s typical homeowner — include trending features like grab bars (up 18%) and wide doorways (up 13%). Less room for kitchens, more flexibility The prominence of chef’s kitchens and gourmet kitchens decreased by 21% and 15%, respectively, suggesting homeowners are willing to trade kitchen space for square footage elsewhere in the home. Meanwhile, mentions of home offices increased 42%, while media rooms rose 37% and flex spaces increased 35%. At the same time, mentions of open concept layouts remain steady. Modern wellness features Wellness features are still important, but not the same ones as years’ past. Cold plunges are decreasingly popular, with mentions falling 44%; similarly, mentions of Jacuzzis and jetted tubs decreased 9%. Instead, buyers are more interested in “spa-inspired” bathrooms, which increased in popularity by 60%. Exercise-related features like golf simulators (up 29%) and home gyms (up 18%) are also trending. Catios Feline friends deserve luxury spaces, too — and now they’re getting them, increasingly more than their canine counterparts. Dog grooming stations fell 16% on Zillow, while mentions of dog parks were stagnant. Instead, catios — screened-in outdoor areas for cats — increased 32%. items.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
items.description: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks.
