items.title: Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. Here’s what comes next.
items.description: Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. Here’s what comes next. by Atlanta Agent November 13, 2026 Anne Hartnett Hi, I'm Anne Hartnett and I am here with real estate economist Matthew Gardner to chat about our Q3 update. How are you, Matthew? Matthew Gardner I am well, Anne, how are you? Hartnett I'm great, thanks. So we've been waiting years for housing transactions to recover. At what point do we stop calling this a cyclical showdown and recognize that something more fundamental has changed in how Americans buy and sell homes? Gardner Great question. I mean, the short answer, as far as I'm concerned, is that we should have stopped calling it a cycle, or cyclical, about a year ago, because the forces that are holding sales down now aren't really the kind that are cycle-fixes. So let me explain. When existing home sales, we know, fell from over 6 million a year in 2021 to about 4 million in 2023, and they've been stuck there for nearly three years now. September numbers came in at 3.99 million. Now, there are three structural forces that explain this: One, the mortgage rate itself has become an asset that people just won't sell. I mean, in the second quarter, 49% of outstanding mortgages carried a rate at below 4%. Now, a record 43% were originated between mid-2019 and mid-2022. That means that selling gives up that loan — and that's not a cycle. It's a balance sheet decision, and it decays very slowly. There are some who suggest that the share of mortgages at 6% or higher, which is around 22.5% in Q2, only hits 27% to 29% by mid-2027. That's a slow grind. Now secondly, the buyer pool has aged. Last year, a typical first-time buyer was 40 years old, and a typical repeat buyer was 62. And last year, first-time buyers were 21% of purchases. That's a record low, and roughly half of their pre-2008 share. And a market that runs on equity rather than income, well, it transacts less often. And finally, the ten year Treasury, it's running around 5% today, and the 3% mortgage was a product of a zero-rate world that no reasonable forecast brings back. But this year, it gave us a small test of my belief. Briefly, back in February, mortgage rates dropped to below 6%, just. I think it was at the end of February. Lowest rate since 2022. But by June, they were back up to 6.5. Now they're above 7.3. Now, at that point, when they were very low, NAR had forecast a 14% jump in sales. But what are we doing today? We're running below last year. So the dip was far too brief to prove anything by itself. But in a normal cycle, cheaper money brings buyers back fast. This time it didn't. So the bottom line for me is that 6 million sales a year is the wrong benchmark. 2021 was an anomaly — a once-in-50-year financing, or refinancing, window. In 2019, we sold about 5.3 million existing homes. And my view is that the realistic norm, at least for the rest of this decade? Somewhere between 4 and 4.5 million. And we'll get there through life events such as job changes, divorce, death, downsizing, not through a rate rally. So for brokers, that changes their business model. In a 4 million-unit market, well, the pipeline isn't buyers waiting for rates to fall. It's people who have to move regardless of rate — relocations, estate sales, divorces, retirees. Now those transactions happen at 7%. If your marketing is built around a quote, wait for rates to drop, unquote, well, you're building for a market, unfortunately, that may not show up. Hartnett Housing drives everything from construction and lending to consumer spending. Could several years of depressed transaction volume begin to weigh on broader economic growth? Gardner It already has, but interestingly, not in the way that most people assume. So let's start with what counts. The sale of an existing home is just a transfer of an asset. It doesn't add to GDP or growth. What counts is construction, remodeling and also the services around a transaction — that would be brokerage commissions, and also households buying new furniture, new appliances, that follow any move. Residential investment is only 3.7% of GDP against a historic average of about five. Now, housing’s total share of the economy? About 16%. That's actually still the lowest we've seen since 2019. Now, residential investment shrank for five straight quarters, falling at an annual rate of about 7.8% in Q1. It did tick up a bit in the second quarter. So no doubt housing has been a drag. But the contrarian part is that the economy grew right through it. Nonresidential investment rose 8.5% in the second quarter, driven by AI equipment and also software. Consumer spending rose 3.4%. You see, homeowners are sitting on substantial equity, and that wealth supports spending even when they don't move. Low transactional volumes is a slow leak, not a recession trigger. Now the real risk, as I see it, is actually different. Housing's historically been the economy's shock absorber. A recession hits the Fed cuts rates to stimulate the economy, ultimately mortgage rates drop, housing turns and construction hiring leads to a recovery. Now that channel’s impaired. Ten-year treasury near five, inflation at 3.4, and in early October, markets are still weighing whether the Fed's next move could be to hike in order to address inflation. But if the labor market weakens further — now remember, September we added just 29000 jobs — well, the Fed should be cutting rates, but I just don't see that happening. So we may not get the usual housing-led rebound on the other side. Now where you feel the drag first is local and also sectoral. It's not in GDP. It shows up in title, escrow, mortgage originations, moving companies, furniture retailers and obviously broker incomes, but also shows up in city and state budgets. The median sale price was $140,900 per unit, while cap rates have averaged 6.1%.Tucson multifamily market overviewOperating conditions in the Tucson multifamily market continued to stabilize during the third quarter, highlighted by tightening vacancy conditions. At just 7.2%, current vacancies are at their lowest levels since the second half of 2022. Recent improvement has occurred throughout nearly all of Tucson’s submarkets, with the northern portions of the metro generally tightening faster than the rest of the market. items.title: The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force
items.description: Housing inventory Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it's more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027. Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025. Weekly inventory change (Nov. 6-Nov. 13): Inventory fell from 902,740 to 895,988 Same week last year (Nov. 7-Nov. 14): Inventory fell from 842,257 to 836,487 New listings New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 53,162 2025: 56,569 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown. items.description: John Cagigas Email 678-390-3055 Bio and Articles Find Your Next Job ! Commercial Litigation Attorney Paralegal - Washington, Dist. Columbia Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico Explore More Job Openings U.S. Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know by: John Cagigas , Winstead - News Alert Monday, November 9, 2026 Related Practices & Jurisdictions Real Estate Financial Institutions Banking Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Introduction On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 19521 (the “ Act ”). As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes. Homes acquired through statutory exceptions after July 11, 2026, are excluded from that count. For this purpose, a “ single-family home ” generally means a structure with no more than two dwelling units, excluding manufactured homes. On October 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “ Treasury ”) issued proposed regulations under Title X (proposed 31 C.F.R. Part 36, the “ Proposed Regulations ”). The Proposed Regulations explain several exceptions for build-to-rent (“ BTR ”), renovate-to-rent, homeownership programs, creditor enforcement and institutional resales, as well as rules affecting investment funds and managers. However, some of the Treasury’s proposals could also complicate common BTR development and sale structures. As of the date hereof, the Proposed Regulations are not binding or final, and the Treasury expects additional rulemakings. Public comments on the Proposed Regulations will be due by November 23, 2026, and the statutory purchase prohibition under the Act becomes effective January 7, 2027, independent of when final regulations are adopted. Key Takeaways The headline for BTR is mixed: the Treasury proposes a purchase deadline of 18 months after a home receives its certificate of occupancy, but also confirms that qualifying homes can be resold repeatedly between covered institutional investors. The Treasury also proposes a written-program requirement for several exceptions and a more detailed test for passive investors. Important gaps remain that are unresolved in the Proposed Regulations, including how the Act applies to fund aggregation, equity transfers, pre-effective-date purchase contracts and BTR homes leased before an institutional sale. The discussion below distinguishes what Congress expressly provided in the Act from the additional conditions the Treasury now offers in the in the Proposed Regulations. BTR Protection: Greater Certainty, but a Narrower Initial Acquisition Window The Act expressly allows purchases under a BTR program in which a large institutional investor “ purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains ” newly constructed homes to be managed as rentals. Our Initial Article explained why that language appeared to protect traditional BTR development and institutional takeout sales. The Treasury’s proposed definition, however, focuses on when a home is purchased and how it is first occupied. Proposed § 36.5 would require a home acquired under the BTR exception to (i) have no previous owner-occupant, (ii) be purchased within 18 months after its certificate of occupancy (or local equivalent), and (iii) be first occupied by renters after the purchase. The Treasury rejected an alternative that would treat an older home as “ newly constructed ” solely because it was originally built and continuously used as a rental. The proposal does not separately explain how these purchase-focused requirements apply when an institutional investor itself constructs and retains the homes, a scenario the Act expressly includes. This may matter for merchant-builders that deliver a community in phases, lease homes as they are completed and sell the stabilized project in one transaction. Because the proposed deadline is tied to each home’s certificate of occupancy, earlier phases could fall outside the proposed BTR exception even while later phases qualify. The Treasury has not proposed a project-wide extension measured from the final phase or stabilization. Another statutory exception may be needed for homes that miss the 18-month window. A second issue concerns lease-up before closing. The proposed § 36.5(c) states that homes must be “ after the purchase, first occupied by renters .” That language appears to require that first-time rental occupancy occur after the institutional buyer purchases the homes, so a home already renter-occupied before sale would appear ineligible for this exception. The Proposed Regulations do not expressly disqualify pre-leased homes or analyze pre-sale lease-up, so clarification remains warranted before buyers rely on this exception. The Act permits BTR homes in both entirely rental and mixed rental/owner-occupied communities, and the Treasury confirms that the exception is not lost simply because a development also contains other property types. The rule still applies home-by-home: conventional apartment buildings with three or more dwelling units per structure generally fall outside the Act’s definition of “ single-family home ,” while qualifying SFR homes within the same development remain subject to the applicable exception. items.title: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak
items.description: San Diego apartment supply is about to peak by Kim O'Brien Posted November 5, 2026 in Insights San Diego apartment supply hit a record high in the past year and is set to peak in 1st quarter 2027. In the year-ending 3rd quarter 2026, roughly 6,600 units completed across San Diego, marking the highest annual total since Realpage Market Analytics began tracking the market in 2000. Supply in the past year also surpassed the market’s decade average around the 4,000-unit mark. Annual supply in San Diego is expected to remain elevated, peaking in the year-ending 1st quarter 2027, when roughly 6,880 units are scheduled for completion. After that, supply is slated to come down, aligning closer to the market’s decade average by the end of 2027. Demand is keeping pace with record apartment supply in San Diego, as evidenced by occupancy at 95.7% in October and rents up 1.5% year-over-year. After supply hits its peak and starts to come down, this market is projected to see improvement in both of those metrics. items.title: Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls
items.description: America's apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding. National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11. The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%. The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables. Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month. Supply wave cools Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak. Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025. Landlords hit the brakes Improving rents haven't translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust , a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve's rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn. Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined. Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said. Camden's earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company's guidance midpoint. "A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment," Parsons wrote. Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters. Coasts and Midwest lead Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut. Sun Belt still lags Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%. San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%. Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%. items.title: Why the 2026 fake foreclosure crisis never happened
items.description: The 2026 foreclosure crisis that some people predicted has failed to materialize, and now those people look silly. We should be thankful for the regulations and laws enacted that laid the foundation for such a sound housing credit market: The 2005 bankruptcy reform law and the 2010 Dodd-Frank laws that established qualified mortgage guidelines were historically positive for the U.S. economy. Looking at the New York Fed's Household Debt and Credit Report for Q3, we can clearly see that the anticipated foreclosure crisis hasn't happened. All the headlines showing a high percentage of year-over-year growth in foreclosure data didn’t amount to anything near a crisis. For those who expected a situation worse than what we experienced in 2008, it has been an embarrassing year. This highlights the dangers of listening to economic discussions from those without the necessary expertise. So let’s talk about where these doomers get it wrong. The idea that the FHA foreclosure moratorium, which ended in October 2025, would lead to a surge in distressed listings has been a popular topic this year. It's gotten a lot of headlines, but has fallen flat on its face, since that isn’t how the foreclosure-to-listing process works in America. At minimum, it takes 9-18 months from the start of the foreclosure process to finally add that supply to the marketplace. And foreclosure data has not, at any point since 2014, shown any material sign of credit stress building up in the pipeline. Always remember, 1%-4% of all mortgages are always going to be in delinquency; it’s when that data breaks above historical norms that it should get everyone’s attention. To illustrate what a true foreclosure crisis might look like, we can consider the historical context: since World War II, we have experienced 13 recessions with an average unemployment rate of 7.8%, but only one significant foreclosure crisis, which was the run-up to the 2008 Great Recession. It took four years for the foreclosure credit market to build up before the 2008 recession hit. As we finish Q3 of 2026, we still haven't returned to pre-COVID levels of foreclosure credit stress, as the data below has always shown for anyone who believes in reading. The New York Fed foreclosure credit stress data line moves slowly, and unless this index is above 200, there isn't much activity out of the norm. The many posts this year predicting a foreclosure crisis have proven to be exaggerated. The scale of the situation is small, and it's clear that many commentators lack the experience to accurately discuss the current market conditions. Additionally, I want to highlight HousingWire’s new listing data . During the previous housing crisis, credit foreclosures directly impacted new listing data, pushing weekly listings to between 250,000 and 400,000 — for years. These listings represented distressed sellers who were forced to sell in an underwater market. All those increases from 2005-2008 in foreclosures eventually became distressed sales, and none of that is happening today. Let's compare the new listings data for last week to the same week from 2009-2011: 2009: 280,400 new listings 2010: 353,457 new listings 2011: 352,030 new listings 2026: 54,478 new listings We're missing a credit boom/bust The 2008 massive credit boom and bust took many years to create. We have not seen this kind of credit boom in housing from 2010-2026, so it’s impossible to have a credit bust like 2008 — or "worse than 2008," as many untrained fake housing analysts have talked about for years. A lot of people can’t let go of the past, as they’re still dancing with the ghost of the 2008 housing crisis. They should relax, have a glass of wine, and reflect on their bad takes. In contrast, over the last 16 years, FICO scores in America have remained strong. Most homeowners have 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, and qualification guidelines are much more stringent and effective now. Rising wages and homeowners staying in their properties longer have contributed to the overall financial health of American households. Despite claims of an impending foreclosure crisis, the reality is quite different. In 2010, over 23% of homes in America were underwater, with loan-to-value ratios reaching nearly 86% in 2011. Currently, the loan-to-value figure is down to 44.2%, as the chart below shows. It's crucial to be cautious about who you listen to, as the narrative of a looming crisis has been overstated for many years. If someone tells you it’s housing 2008 or a foreclosure crisis is here, tell them to read a book instead of burning it, and read HousingWire. Related More: Foreclosure

items.title: VA default remains low despite record debt
items.description: Low default rates obscure record debt exposure across the expanding VA mortgage market. VA loans drive 9.5% of purchase originations, with average balances tripling to $418,000. Serious delinquency is low at 2.0% (vs. 5.0% for FHA), but record loan sizes amplify dollar risk. Zero-down financing and no monthly mortgage insurance make VA loans a vital hedge against high rates. Veterans are borrowing more money than ever before, and by conventional benchmarks, the VA loans asset class looks remarkably disciplined. According to Cotality data, delinquencies are sitting at a 2.0% — down from a year ago and roughly a third of the 6.5% pandemic peak, and well below the 5.0% recorded across the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) book. But a reassuring percentage can obscure an expensive reality. Low rates, record exposure The volume of distressed veteran mortgage debt is substantially larger than at any point in the last 20 years. In 2005, VA purchase loans were a niche product accounting for just 1.4% of purchase originations. Now they account for nearly ten times that number. VA purchase originations: Count and amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 One in every ten closed loans are VA-funded, which is actually down from their peak popularity in 2021 when VA originations surged near 282,000 loans, generating roughly $100 billion in volume across 2021 and 2022. But alongside the number of loans increasing, the average VA purchase balance has more than tripled, climbing from $122,500 in 1998 to $418,000 in 2026. When the pandemic-era competition recalibrated price ceilings, loan balances accelerated sharply from $286,000 to $355,000 in just two years. That popularity has mathematical consequences. A 2% delinquency on a portfolio of $122,500 loans comprising 1.4% of originations could be written off as an operational blip. But 2% delinquency on a $418,000 baseline across nearly a tenth of the national purchase market translates to billions in non-performing principal. Average VA purchase share by loan count Data source: Cotality, 2026 That risk isn’t due to borrowers failing at a higher rate. The size of VA loan portfolios has simply expanded to the point where small percentage slippages represent significant dollar exposure. Webinar Veteran Homeownership: Turning Service into Generational Wealth Affording stability This dramatic expansion in loan balances was not born of speculation, but of survival in a housing market where affordability is strained. With mortgage rates and home prices at near generational highs, the conventional path to homeownership is bending out of reach for millions . Accumulating a traditional 10% to 20% down payment on the national median home price of $429,450 demands $42,000 to $84,000 in liquid savings—a barrier that sidelines even buyers with comfortable earnings. Average VA purchase loan amount Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ A VA loan offers an achievable alternative. By offering loans with little to no downpayment requirement and eliminating monthly mortgage insurance requirements, this Ginnie Mae-backed option allows eligible service members and veterans to enter the market without draining cash reserves. When income shocks arrive, that liquidity buffer can keep families in their homes. That structural safety net is why VA loans crested at only 6.5% serious delinquency during the 2020 market tumult, while FHA loans spiked to 12.2% *. The defense corridors Because military demographics are highly geographic, this heavy-balance exposure is not even across the country, with clusters appearing in specific regional economies: Alaska: VA financing drives 28% of the funds put towards all home purchase originations. Virginia: VA loans account for 22% of the total dollar amount of all originations. Hawaii: VA transactions 20% of the total dollars that people put toward buying a home ‍ VA purchase dollar amount by state Data source: Cotality, 2026 In these markets, the VA loan is the bedrock of local housing turnover. Any shift in federal loan limits, interest rate trajectories, or military deployment cycles triggers an outsized local shock. The VA loan has become a high-balance, high-volume credit engine. For mortgage originators and servicers, the payment discipline of this population offers security, but the larger loan sizes mean there is far less margin for error when local job markets or regional housing valuations stumble. For servicers and secondary-market investors managing these pools, the priority is no longer just tracking the headline delinquency rate. It is managing the sheer weight of the capital behind it. Webinar Veteran Homeownership: Turning Service into Generational Wealth *The CARES Act provided forbearance for borrowers with federally backed mortgage loans who were economically impacted by the pandemic. Borrowers in a forbearance program who have missed a mortgage payment are included in the Cotality delinquency statistics, even if the loan servicer has not reported the loan as delinquent to credit repositories Property market economics Mortgage banking & financial technology Housing affordability

items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: The math behind staying put: When does buying a home beat renting?
items.description: The math behind staying put: When does buying a home beat renting? by Arben Skivjani Posted November 2, 2026 in Rent Growth Rate In January 2021, mortgage rates hit a record low of 2.65%. On October 29, 2026, Freddie Mac’s 30-year rate was 7.24%, more than a full point higher than a year ago. Including property taxes and insurance, the monthly cost of owning the typical home now runs about $930 more than the rent on an average apartment. A difference that size drives a lot of decisions in the apartment market, starting with whether renters keep renting or buy a home. So how far would rates have to fall for the two to even out? Farther than most people think. To see how we got here, I went back to four moments when the math looked very different, from the high rates of 2000 to the record lows of 2021, and followed a household earning the median income through each one. At each moment, I compared the monthly loan payment on a typical home, using a 30-year fixed mortgage with 20% down, with the rent on an average apartment. On that basis alone, today’s payment of about $2,300 runs nearly $380 above the $1,915 average rent in our data. Taxes and insurance make up the rest, and I’ll get to those. Through all four moments, renters have been responding to the math. In our data, they’re renewing more often than they did 20 years ago, and today they’re signing the longest renewal leases since our records began in 2002. 2000 and 2006: A much smaller gap In the spring of 2000, the 30-year rate was about 8.3%, the kind of number that would stop most buyers today. But homes were cheaper relative to incomes. The median single-family home sold for about $144,000, according to the National Association of Realtors, or about 3.4 times the median household income. The monthly payment came to about $870, only about $40 more than the average rent in our data, and took about 25% of the Census Bureau’s median household income. Six years later, near the peak of the housing boom, the math had shifted. Rates had eased, but the median price had climbed to $220,000. The payment now ran about $160 above average rent. The difference had grown, but for many households it was still manageable. The down payment had grown, too, from more than two-thirds of a year’s median income in 2000 to more than 90% by 2006. Meanwhile, apartment occupancy slipped from 96% to just under 95%, after years of easy credit had pulled many renters into homeownership. 2012: Owning costs less than renting After the housing crash, the picture flipped. By the end of 2012, the median home had fallen to about $181,000, and the 30-year rate had dropped to about 3.4%. The monthly payment was about $410 less than average rent and took only 15% of median income, the lowest share of the five moments. On paper, owning was clearly the cheaper choice. In practice, it wasn’t that simple. Lenders had tightened their standards after the crisis, and saving a 20% down payment was still a big hurdle. Residents were already renewing more often, 49% at the end of 2012, up from 46% in 2006. For a lot of households, the math on paper and the reality didn’t line up. 2021: The cheapest money on record Then came the pandemic, and with it record-low mortgage rates. Home prices were climbing fast, with the median at about $335,000 in early 2021, but with rates under 3%, the monthly payment was still more than $300 below average rent. At 19% of median income, the payment was easy to manage for a typical household. It was a strong time for apartments, too. Job growth came back quickly, and apartment demand surged. By early 2022, occupancy in our data had climbed to 97.5%, the highest going back to 2000. Cheap mortgages and a strong rental market existed side by side, because the economy was creating new households fast enough to fill both. That window didn’t stay open for long. As inflation picked up, the Fed began raising rates in 2022, and mortgage rates followed. By the end of that year, the 30-year rate was above 6%, and households that had waited to buy faced a very different payment on a similar home. Many decided to keep renting. 2026: The widest gap of the five Today, rates and prices are both pushing the cost of owning higher. The median home sells for about $420,000, roughly 25% more than in early 2021, and the mortgage rate is more than twice as high. That puts the monthly loan payment at about $2,300, roughly 20% above average rent. Even in 2006, near the peak of the boom, the payment ran only about 16% above rent. For a family earning the median household income, about $87,500 a year, that payment would take nearly a third of their income, up from 15% in 2012 and above the 30% line that lenders and housing economists often use as a sign of strain. The home itself costs about 4.8 times their annual income, the highest multiple of the five moments. Add property taxes and insurance, and owning looks even more expensive. Using a national average effective property tax rate of 0.9%, according to ATTOM, and an average homeowners insurance premium of about $2,900 a year, according to Insurance.com, the full monthly cost of owning the median home comes to about $2,840. That’s about $930 above average rent, before a single repair bill. Then there’s the down payment. Twenty percent down on today’s median home is about $84,000, nearly a full year of median household income and the highest share of the five moments. It’s no surprise that the typical first-time buyer is now 40 years old, according to the National Association of Realtors, and that first-time buyers made up just 21% of purchases, a record low. Renters are staying put Renters are doing the same math, and it shows. In Realpage data, 57% of renters whose leases were up in the third quarter of 2026 chose to renew, compared with 46% back in 2006. And when they renew, they’re signing on for longer. items.title: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms
items.description: October 2026 CPI: Inflation Firms, December Fed Hike Looms By Jake Krimmel Nov 10, 2026 October's consumer price index came in a touch hotter than forecasters expected, with headline inflation up 0.4% on the month and core up 0.3%. Because of last year's government shutdown, BLS did not publish annual rates, but the details show inflation remains broad-based. December Fed hike odds jumped to 99% and the 10-year Treasury yield moved higher, putting new upward pressure on mortgage rates after three straight weekly declines. Here's what today's report means for the Fed, consumers, and the housing market. October 2026 CPI at a Glance Headline CPI: +0.4% MoM Seasonally Adjusted (SA), following September's +0.6% rise, versus forecasts of +0.2% to +0.3%; BLS did not publish an annual rate because October 2025 data were not collected during the government shutdown Core CPI (less food & energy): +0.3% MoM (SA), matching September and August, versus a forecast of +0.2% Energy: +0.7% MoM (SA) after +5.2% in September; gasoline +1.0% MoM (SA) and +37.4% YoY Food: +0.5% MoM (SA), with food at home up 0.4% and food away from home up 0.5% Shelter: +0.3% MoM (SA) after +0.4% in September, with rent up 0.2% and owners' equivalent rent up 0.3% Real earnings: real average hourly earnings were unchanged, as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation Fed outlook: odds of a December hike jumped to 99%, with Governor Waller's comments putting a 50 basis point move on the table Market reaction: the 10-year Treasury yield was up 9 basis points 25 minutes after the release Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac's 30-year rate fell to 7.18% in the week of November 5, the third straight weekly decline, after peaking at 7.4% in October October CPI: a touch hotter than expected, and inflation remains broad-based October’s CPI came in a touch hotter than consensus, with headline up 0.4% month over month (versus a forecasted 0.2 to 0.3%) and core inflation rising 0.3% month over month compared to an expected 0.2%. These figures hardly qualify as a shock to markets or the outlook, but the details of the report show inflation remains broad-based, with food, energy, shelter, and vehicles all up, to name a few. The BLS did not publish annual rates because of last year’s government shutdown, but headline inflation likely remains in the high 3s. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. What it means for the Fed: a December hike looks almost certain The same supply-side and geopolitical pressures are still at work, with energy playing an important role and tariff-driven goods inflation not going away. These are the costs most salient to consumers and voters, as we saw, yet the Fed has less direct control over them. On the Fed outlook, a December hike now looks almost certain, with odds jumping to 99% this morning . That market reaction is both due to the warmer than anticipated CPI print and Governor Waller’s comments (which occurred prior to the CPI report) putting a 50 basis point move on the table for December. Additional hikes in early 2027 look more in play as well, with the 10-year Treasury up 9 basis points just 25 minutes after the CPI report release. What it means for housing: mortgage rates could turn higher again For housing in the near term, we could see upward pressure on mortgage rates again. After three straight weekly declines to 7.18% , rising Treasury yields and growing speculation about hikes in early 2027 could reverse that trend. October’s spike to 7.4% showed how quickly higher rates hurt demand, with contract signings and new listings each falling about 10% from September as buyers and sellers pulled back . Rate swings grab the headlines and matter for the marginal buyer, but the real wage squeeze is a longer-run, underexplored headwind for demand. Real average hourly earnings were flat in October as 0.4% wage growth matched 0.4% inflation, leaving annual real wage growth negative for buyers already facing mortgage rates above 7% .

items.title: Hot Inflation Report and Hawkish Comments From Fed’s Waller Put a 50 Bps December Hike in Play
items.description: Hot Inflation Report and Hawkish Comments From Fed’s Waller Put a 50 Bps December Hike in Play Published on November 10th, 2026 by Chen Zhao Takeaway: A hot inflation report coupled with aggressive remarks from Fed Governor Waller overnight locks in a December rate hike and brings up the possibility of a larger 50 bps hike or a previously unanticipated hike in January. Core CPI, which excludes energy and food, came in at 0.296% month-over-month in October, down from the previous month, but higher than the forecasted 0.22%. Overall CPI came in at 0.350% month-over-month, also higher than the forecasted 0.25%. The inflationary pressure appears to be broad-based in this report, not coming from any single outlier category. Though there might be a small boost because of a distortion in how the Bureau of Labor Statistics seasonally adjusts this data after the government shutdown last year. Today’s data means the December 9th rate hike, which has been priced in, is definitely going to happen. The question now is whether they go 25 bps or a larger than usual 50 bps. Overnight Fed Governor Christopher Waller gave a speech in London saying “ But if the October CPI inflation data … are similar to the past two monthly readings—with core CPI inflation around 0.3 percent or even higher—then a stronger policy move may be needed. In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take. ” Lots of other Fed officials are on the calendar to speak later this week. The question now is whether they also support a 50 bps hike or if they would prefer to put a previously unanticipated January hike on the table instead. The latter may be preferable because going 50 bps after skipping a hike at the October meeting may look unusual. The key takeaway from this analysis is that luxury prices continue to soften, with the entry-level luxury price dipping 2.3% from a year ago in October. items.title: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices
items.description: October Marks the First Month in 3 Years With a Decline in U.S. Home-Sale Prices Published on November 10th, 2026 by Dana Anderson The median U.S. home-sale price fell in October for the first time in over 3 years. Prices are still rising rapidly in some metros with hot markets, including San Francisco, where they rose 16.8% year over year, and the greater New York City area. Home sales fell as mortgage rates surpassed 7%–but flattening prices could bring buyers a bit of relief. Would-be sellers are starting to pull back as demand declines, but the total number of homes for sale climbed to its highest level since 2020. For three years, U.S. home-sale prices rose from a year earlier every single month, even as mortgage rates climbed and would-be buyers pulled back. That streak has ended. The median home-sale price declined 0.4% year over year to $388,634 in October. That’s the first decline since May 2023 and a sharp slowdown from the 2.5% gain just two months earlier. With Americans’ wages growing about 4% year over year , even a slight dip in prices can improve affordability. Sale prices have risen nearly every single month for the last 13 years; the only exception was a handful of months in 2023. With the total number of homes for sale at its highest level since early 2020 and demand cooling, homebuyers’ negotiating power keeps increasing–and that’s finally showing up in sale prices. Home Prices Are Still Rising Fast in Hot Markets, Led By San Francisco Home-sale prices fell nationwide, but they rose in more than half of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas. San Francisco led the nation by a wide margin, with the median sale price rising 16.8% year over year. That’s the biggest increase since 2018. Next comes New Brunswick, NJ, with a 7.7% gain. Two other NYC-area metros also had price increases ranking in the top six; the median sale price rose 4.4% in both New York City and Nassau County. In San Francisco, AI wealth is fueling competition for scarce inventory; active listings were down 7% from a year earlier. In the New York City area, years of limited homebuilding have left buyers competing for relatively few homes in a region with a strong job market. Home-sale prices fell most in Austin, TX, where they declined 6.5% year over year. It’s followed by Seattle (-5.1%) and Nashville, TN (-4.9%). Austin and Nashville are among the biggest buyer’s markets in the U.S., and Seattle’s shaky tech job market is curbing demand . U.S. Pending Home Sales Drop to Lowest Level Since the Pandemic National sale prices are losing steam because fewer Americans can afford to buy a home. U.S. pending home sales fell 3.6% from a month earlier in October on a seasonally adjusted basis to their lowest level since 2013, with the exception of April 2020. This is a real-time indicator of the state of the housing market; fewer homes went under contract in October largely because mortgage rates averaged 7.33% , a three-year high and up from 6.86% the month before. All figures in this report are seasonally adjusted, with the exception of median sale price data and mortgage rate data. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here . “It’s a buyer’s market, but not many people can afford to buy,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics. “That could start to shift a bit, now that sale prices are closer to reflecting the shape of the market. House hunters in most of the country should know that the price they see on a listing may very well be a starting point; they should try offering below the asking price, and negotiating for closing costs, repairs and maybe even mortgage-rate buydowns. If you can’t get the price or monthly payment you want on one house, move on to the next one–with a big pool of inventory sitting on the market, buyers can afford to be picky.” Pending home sales declined in all of the most populous U.S. metros. That’s the second month in a row that has happened; before September, the last time was three years earlier. The biggest declines were in Seattle and San Diego, both places where pending sales fell more than 20% year over year. Those West Coast metros are some of the priciest in the U.S., so 7%-plus mortgages hit house hunters’ monthly payments there hard. In Seattle, an uncertain local job market is also curbing demand . Closed home sales fell to their lowest level in nearly 3 years. They declined 2.1% month over month in October to their lowest level since December 2023; before that, the last time sales dropped that low was 2014. Many of the deals that closed last month went under contract in August and September, when rates were already climbing and economic uncertainty was deterring a lot of house hunters. Housing Supply Builds to Highest Level Since 2020 With homebuying demand falling, supply is building. The total number of homes for sale rose 0.9% from September to its highest level since early 2020; that’s the biggest monthly gain since May 2025. More supply gives buyers more homes to choose from and more leverage: Three in five homes are selling under asking price. 61% of homes that sold in October went for less than their original list price. More sellers are cutting their prices. 36% of homes that sold in October had at least one price drop–the highest share in our records. Roughly 15% of pending sales fell out of contract. items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Named Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for Fifth Consecutive Year, Expands Veteran Career Pathways Nationwide Phoebe Schmidt • 11/11/2026 Veteran's Day 2026 New York -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) announced today that the real estate services firm has been recognized as a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year. As the nation celebrates America's 250th anniversary, the firm continues expanding opportunities for veterans transitioning to civilian careers, with a particular focus on skilled trades and technical professions. "As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, we're reminded that the country's strength has always depended on people willing to serve something larger than themselves," said Bruce Mosler , Chairman of Global Brokerage. "Veterans leave the military with experience leading teams, solving problems under pressure and taking responsibility when the stakes are high. Those qualities are increasingly difficult to find and impossible to teach overnight. Creating opportunities for veterans isn't simply a way to honor their service. It's an investment in the future workforce and leadership of this country." Cushman & Wakefield employs more than 1,400 veterans across its U.S. operations and has plans to hire an additional 500 veterans this year. Through its Military & Veterans Programs, the firm provides recruitment, mentorship and career-transition support, including participation in the Department of War's SkillBridge program and military spouse employment initiatives. The firm's approach to veteran hiring and engagement has also been shared with more than 300 companies nationwide as a model for building effective post-military career pathways. The opportunity is significant. U.S. employers reported approximately 325,000 job openings in construction and 608,000 in manufacturing in July 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. More than 160,000 people leave military service annually with experience maintaining aircraft, vehicles, facilities, electrical systems and heavy equipment. These capabilities can translate directly to civilian careers, including building engineering, HVAC, facilities operations and project management. To help veterans and military spouses explore careers in the skilled trades, Cushman & Wakefield partnered with 50strong in September to launch the Skilled Trades Mentor Hub. They understand how to adapt when technology changes because they've been doing it throughout their military careers. As employers look for talent that can learn quickly, solve problems and operate in high-consequence environments, veterans are exceptionally well positioned to help lead that transformation across industries." In addition to being named a Top Ten Military Friendly® Employer for the fifth consecutive year, the firm was recently recognized as one of America's Most Patriotic Companies 2026 by Newsweek for its support of veterans, service members and military-connected communities. It's proof that honoring military talent is not only the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do." items.title: Building Material Price Inflation Remains High Despite Energy Price Declines
items.description: Building Material Price Inflation Remains High Despite Energy Price Declines November 13, 2026 Jesse Wade No Comments The Producer Price Index for final demand was up 0.3% in October, after rising 1.4% in September. Compared to a year ago, final demand prices were up 6.5%. The price of goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged over the month and up 9.8% from last year, while the price of services was up 0.7% over the month and up 11.3% from last year. Combining goods and services, the price index for inputs to new residential construction was up 0.3% in October and 10.4% higher than last year. Input Goods The goods component has a larger importance to the inputs to residential construction price index, representing around 60% of the total. On a monthly basis, the price of input goods to new residential construction was unchanged in October after rising 1.7% in September. The input goods to residential construction index can be further broken down into two separate components, one measuring energy inputs with the other measuring remaining goods. The latter of these two components simply represents building materials used in residential construction, which makes up around 93% of the goods index. Energy input prices fell 3.3% in October and were 64.8% higher than a year ago. Building material prices were up 0.5% in October and up 5.8% compared to one year ago. Energy prices fell monthly as No. 2 diesel fuel prices fell 4.6% over the month but was a substantial 115.2% higher than a year ago. Outside of energy products, particleboard and fiberboard prices rose 5.4% over the month and were up 13.9% from a year ago. Softwood veneer and plywood prices were up 3.6% over the month and 24.5% higher than a year ago. Input Services Prices for service inputs to residential construction rose 0.7% in October. On a year-over-year basis, service input prices were up 11.3%. The price index for service inputs to residential construction can be broken out into three separate components: a trade services component, a transportation and warehousing services component, and a services excluding trade, transportation, and warehousing component (other services). The most significant component is trade services (around 60%), followed by other services (around 29%), and finally transportation and warehousing services (around 11%). The largest component, trade services, was up 13.2% from a year ago. The price of transportation and warehousing services has risen 24.6% from a year ago, while prices for other services were up 3.0% over the year. items.title: Consumer Credit Growth Picks Up in the Third Quarter of 2026
items.description: Consumer Credit Growth Picks Up in the Third Quarter of 2026 November 10, 2026 Onnah Dereski No Comments Consumer credit growth accelerated in the third quarter of 2026, with both revolving and nonrevolving credit increasing at their fastest quarterly rates since 2022. Total outstanding consumer credit reached $5.22 trillion, continuing an upward trend that has strengthened over the past year. The acceleration comes amid elevated borrowing costs, although interest rates on both auto loans and credit cards continue to edge lower. According to the Federal Reserve’s G.19 Consumer Credit Report , total outstanding U.S. consumer credit reached $5.22 trillion in the third quarter of 2026. This marked a 4.21% increase at a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) from the second quarter, the highest quarterly increase since 2022. Compared to a year ago, total outstanding credit increased 3.01%, the highest growth rate in three years. Nonrevolving Credit Nonrevolving credit, which is primarily made up of student and auto loans (the G.19 report excludes mortgage loans), reached $3.86 trillion (SA) in the third quarter of 2026. This marks a 4.22% increase (SAAR) from the previous quarter, the highest quarterly increase since 2022. Additionally, nonrevolving credit rose 2.57% compared to one year ago, continuing the upward trend over the last five quarters. Student loans make up the largest share of nonrevolving credit, accounting for 49% of the total. In the third quarter of 2026, outstanding student loan credit reached $1.88 trillion (NSA), up 2.81% from a year earlier. The other large component of nonrevolving credit is auto loans. Auto loans reached a level of $1.59 trillion (NSA), showing a year-over-year increase of 1.89%, the largest increase in the last ten quarters. Auto loan rates for a 60-month new car stood at 7.54% (NSA) for the third quarter of 2026, 10 basis points lower than a year ago. Auto loan rates have continued to decline year-over-year for the last eight quarters but remain higher than pre-pandemic levels. Revolving Credit Revolving credit, which is primarily made up of credit card balances, rose to $1.37 trillion (SA) in the third quarter of 2026. This represents a 4.21% increase (SAAR) from the previous quarter and a 4.25% increase year-over-year. Although credit card rates have hovered near historic highs since Q4 2022, they have shown modest year-over-year declines over the past seven quarters. items.title: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math
items.description: The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math Published on November 12th, 2026 by Dana Anderson , Yingqi Xu and Szu Yu Chen Timing made a big difference for millennials. Those who bought a home before 2022 locked in historically low mortgage rates. But those who bought after rates and prices surged spent about 35% of their income on housing–and many other millennials were priced out entirely. Baby boomers had a brutal start, with double-digit mortgage rates in the early 1980s, but falling rates gave them decades to refinance. When boomers were in their late 30s, they spent just over 25% of their income on housing. The typical monthly payment was about $3,000 when elder millennials were 40 to 44 (2021 to 2025), versus about $1,986 for boomers at those ages, in today’s dollars. Millennials earn more than boomers did at the same age in today’s dollars, partly because more women are in the workforce, but housing costs more than cancel out the difference. If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home . For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent. The story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation. Boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000. Key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments. This is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology. Millennials Had an Early Homebuying Advantage In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb. Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage. Then the Math Changed The millennial advantage didn't last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income. Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age. “For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019 , which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing

items.title: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens
items.description: Household Debt Delinquencies Rise as Mortgage Performance Weakens November 11, 2026 Catherine Koh No Comments Household debt delinquency rates increased in the third quarter of 2026 as the share of delinquent balances and the transition to seriously delinquent debt increased. According to the latest Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, about 5.0% of outstanding household debt balances were in some stage of delinquency, an increase of 0.3 percentage points (pp) from the previous quarter. Total household debt balances that were seriously delinquent (at least 90 days delinquent) also edged up slightly from 3.3% in the second quarter to 3.4%. The deterioration occurred across several consumer loan categories. The serious delinquency rate for auto loans increased 0.2 pp to 5.7%, while mortgage delinquency rate increased 0.1 pp to 1.1%. In contrast, the serious delinquency rate for credit cards edged lower to 12.9%, although credit cards continued to have the highest rate among the major debt categories. Student loans displayed continued deterioration. The share of student loan balances that were seriously delinquent increased to 10.9%, from 10.6% in the second quarter. This marked a further increase in the proportion of student loan debt classified as seriously delinquent following the resumption of delinquency reporting. The flow of balances newly entering a serious delinquency stage showed a more mixed picture. Overall, 2.6% transitioned into serious delinquency during the third quarter, unchanged from the previous quarter. The share of student loan balances transitioning into serious delinquency declined to 7.7%, from 7.8% in the previous quarter. This followed a much sharper decline in the second quarter, when the transition rate dropped from 10.9% to 7.8%. Credit card transitions also improved slightly. The share of credit card balances newly entering serious delinquency decreased to 6.9%, from 7.0% in the second quarter, marking the third consecutive quarterly decline. Mortgage transitions, however, continued to move in the opposite direction. The share of mortgage balances newly entering serious delinquency increased to 1.6%, from 1.5% in the previous quarter. This category has been gradually trending upward in recent years, indicating continued deterioration in mortgage credit performance. Auto loan transitions remained relatively steady at 3.0%. items.title: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year
items.description: ARMs hit record 17% of locks: Pitch beyond the 30-year By Spencer Lee CloseText About Spencer twitter Spencer_NYC linkedin spencer-lee-journo Published November 10, 2026, 1:57 p.m. EST | Updated November 10, 2026, 2:06 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email What's at Stake: Homebuyers seeking immediate affordability relief who risk facing severe sticker shock. Expert Quote: "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market." — Brennan O'Connell, Director of Data Solutions, Optimal Blue Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. A growing share of borrowers flocked to adjustable-rate mortgages in October, providing clues about where business may lie as well as the impact that the current economic environment is having on consumer behavior. The share of adjustable-rate mortgage locks last month hit 17%, the highest since the data was first tracked in 2019, according to Optimal Blue's Market Advantage Report. The ARM portion of locks rose from 14% one month earlier. Processing Content The new high mark came at the same time total rate-lock volume tumbled 19% from September and 38% on a year-over-year basis, with numbers falling across all loan categories amid ongoing macroeconomic pressures . Purchase lock volume decreased to an 84% share, relative to total activity, with demand slipping 18% and 17% from the prior month and year. The downward pressure across loan types led Optimal Blue's market volume index to plummet to a reading of 77 compared to 94 in September. "October's data show how much affordability is shaping the purchase market," said Brennan O'Connell, director of data solutions at Optimal Blue, in a press release. In other data showing the momentum currently boosting ARMs, the Mortgage Bankers Association reported lenders expanded availability of such financing for borrowers, especially those with lower loan-to-value ratios compared with recent history. The offerings helped push MBA's Mortgage Credit Availability Index higher for the first time in three months. The trends suggest that opportunities in today's subdued housing market exist outside the standard fixed-rate loan as long as originators can work with borrowers to find solutions that fit individual needs. ARM originations have historically risen when fixed rates surge, providing buyers with affordability relief for at least the first few years of their mortgage. The loans come with an initial fixed interest rate lower than the 30-year average. "For lenders, that means the opportunity is increasingly in helping borrowers find the product and payment structure that works for their circumstances," O'Connell said. Supporting its findings, Optimal Blue pointed out Federal Housing Administration-backed loans also accounted for an expanding percentage of mortgage locks, and first-time homebuyers grew in the agency market. The FHA segment made up 20% of locks, while Department of Veterans Affairs-backed mortgages took an 11% share, both up from September. Meanwhile, conforming loans made up 46% of all October locks, while non-conforming transactions accounted for 22%, both declining from the prior month. First-time buyers nabbed 45% of conforming purchase locks, climbing from both the previous month and year. Non-qualified mortgages, which are also experiencing heightened demand this year, made up 12% of October loan production, edging down from September but up by 195 basis points over the past three months and 420 basis points year over year. Non-QM lock volume split in close-to-equivalent shares between debt service coverage ratio, bank-statement and expanded guideline programs. Mortgage lenders see expanded credit availability The MBA's credit index increased 0.4% between September and October to a reading of 107.5, in part due to elevated ARM interest, with higher marks indicative of a greater number of products. In September, the MCAI settled at a score of 107.1, with a benchmark of 100 representing credit availability in March 2012, following the Great Recession. Unlike Optimal Blue's findings, though, government-product availability flattened, while conventional offerings grew, MBA reported. The uptick in ARM loans with lower LTV ratios included cash-out refinancing products, according to the trade association. "This also boosted the jumbo index, which was up to its highest level in three months," said Joel Kan, MBA vice president and deputy chief economist. The conventional MCAI increased 0.6%, while the government index grew by just 0.1%. Subindices within the conventional component showed jumbo offerings up 0.8% month to month and conforming credit unchanged. Look out for ARM regret Although lenders will appreciate the activity boosting their bottom line, recent history suggests consumers may want to approach them with caution. Research conducted in 2024 found approximately 70% of ARM borrowers expressed regret about their choice , with some facing sticker shock when the initial fixed term ended. items.title: Cushman & Wakefield Announces Sale of Historic 121 W. Wacker to Chicago-Based Investor Group
items.description: Cushman & Wakefield Announces Sale of Historic 121 W. Wacker to Chicago-Based Investor Group Jeremy Barewin • 11/10/2026 Cushman & Wakefield Retained as Exclusive Leasing Agent 121 W. Wacker, Chicago CHICAGO -- Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK), a leading global real estate services firm, today announced the sale of 121 W. Wacker, a landmark 41-story office tower overlooking the Chicago River and located at the gateway to Chicago's historic LaSalle Street corridor. The 441,030-square-foot property was acquired by two Chicago-based investors Ken Buckman and Robert Castillo, who intend to invest substantial capital to re-energize the nearly century-old building. Cushman & Wakefield's Cody Hundertmark and Tom Sitz represented the seller, Chicago-based real estate firm Ameritus, in the transaction. Following the acquisition, Cushman & Wakefield has been retained as the exclusive leasing agent for the property, with Mason Taylor and Paige Krueger leading leasing efforts. Unlike many institutional office investors, the principals come from business entrepreneurship and private equity. Their vision for the property's next chapter centers on long-term ownership, thoughtful modernization and renewing its prominence as one of downtown Chicago's enduring architectural landmarks. "Owning 121 W. Wacker is about much more than acquiring a real estate asset," said Buckman. "As Chicago residents, we felt strongly that 121 W. Wacker should remain in local hands. The property has a remarkable history, an irreplaceable location and a presence in the Chicago skyline that deserves thoughtful stewardship. We have ambitious plans to modernize the tenant experience while preserving the character and architectural details that make this one of the city's great buildings." The ownership group is planning a series of capital improvements to position the tower for the needs of today's leading companies. Enhancements include a significant upgrade to the outdoor amenity terrace and 24th floor conference center, a completely remodeled restaurant and bar managed by a leading Chicago hospitality firm and a refreshed main lobby experience. Award-winning international design firm Ware Malcomb will oversee all interior and exterior architecture, with Ameritus continuing as the building's property manager. Situated at the intersection of Wacker Drive and LaSalle Street, the property offers sweeping views of the Chicago River and skyline, immediate access to the Chicago Riverwalk and multiple public transportation options. The location places it amid the growing residential and business activity reshaping the Loop, just one block from Google's new Chicago headquarters, scheduled to open next year. "121 W. Wacker remains one of the most distinctive office buildings in downtown Chicago, offering something that cannot be replicated: authentic architectural character in an unmatched riverfront location," said Mason Taylor, Executive Managing Director, Agency Leasing at Cushman & Wakefield. "The new ownership group brings an entrepreneurial mindset, a genuine commitment to Chicago and a willingness to invest in the building's future. With planned upgrades throughout the property, it is exceptionally well-positioned to attract companies seeking a premier office environment, centrally located along Wacker Drive." Completed in 1930 and designed by renowned Chicago architects Holabird & Root, 121 W. Wacker stands as one of the city's most recognizable Art Deco skyscrapers. Originally known as the LaSalle-Wacker Building, the tower helped establish the northern gateway to Chicago's historic financial district and was among the last major buildings constructed in the city before the Great Depression. Now included within the West Loop-LaSalle Street Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places, the building has witnessed nearly a century of Chicago's evolution, with early ties to two iconic companies, United Airlines and McDonald's, both of which once maintained offices at the property. About Cushman & Wakefield Cushman & Wakefield (NYSE: CWK) is a leading global commercial real estate services firm for occupiers and investors with approximately 53,000 employees in over 350 offices and nearly 60 countries. In 2025, the firm reported revenue of $10.3 billion across its core service lines of Services, Leasing, Capital markets, and Valuation and other. Built around the belief that Better never settles , the firm receives numerous industry and business accolades for its award-winning culture.
